title: House of the Dead
full_review:
When combining a former music video director and a script based on an ultraviolent video game involving flesh-eating zombies, the question that should immediately form in one's mind is not "Will the resulting movie be bad?" but rather "Just how bad will it be?" In the case of "House of the Dead" (Artisan), the answer is painfully, inexplicably, run-screaming-back-to-the-ticket-booth-and-demand-your-money-back bad.

"House of the Dead" -- which pretty much describes the funereal hush of the empty theaters this film would, in a just world, play to -- is a relentlessly ridiculous gorefest about a group of party-seeking college coeds trapped on an island infested with blood-sucking ghouls and stockpiled with lots of ammo. Directed by Ewe Boll, the film is so laughable that, if not for its incessant violence, peppered with gratuitous nudity, it could more accurately be marketed as a comedy.

Lured to the aptly named Isla del Muerte by an invitation to a rave party, the preternaturally good-looking zombie-fodder hitch a ride aboard the boat of a German gunrunner named Captain Kirk (Jurgen Prochnow). Kirk's stooge sidekick is played -- with equally embarrassing results -- by serial hack Clint Howard, who braves his humiliation dressed up like the Gorton's fisherman. Once on the mysterious island, however, they find out that whoever booked the place forgot to inquire about the flesh-eating undead locals who have a habit of crashing keg parties.

After the oversexed troupe hook up with some stray revelers holed up in the island's creepy cemetery and a Rambo-esque female Coast Guard officer (Ellie Cornell), the film nosedives from garden-variety schlock to a progressively sadistic bloodbath, intercut with violent video-game images. The lavishly grotesque action leads nowhere, stumbling aimlessly toward a ludicrous climax with the island's zombie impresario -- a 17th-century Spanish priest-turned-necromancer.

The film opens with the sole survivor pondering, "It all started when I came here for a rave, and it ended with the rotting smell of death." Needless to say, the stink he is referring to is coming from the projection booth.

The decorative, mostly no-name cast is so wooden that theatres should provide tweezers so viewers can remove splinters after each showing. Of course, such rigor mortis is to be expected when the dialogue and characterizations are less fleshed-out than the partially decomposed islanders.

In the film's closing hopeful-dawn-after-a-night-of-bloody-mayhem scene, a helicopter swoops down from the sky. The dazed survivor asks the pilot who he is, to which the pilot responds, "I'm here to rescue you." Unfortunately for anyone caught watching this turkey, he's about two hours too late.

Due to excessive graphic carnage, extended topless nudity, lewd humor, pervasive rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
